name: Liam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a building-site crew fitting window frames and facade panels. My vocational trade certificate got me started, and I am good at the awkward openings, though my pay is the ordinary trade rate. I like seeing a weatherproof seal at handover; late glass deliveries steal the daylight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in care, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We've saved about three months of expenses, and there are some other construction jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to read a long specification, but I want a colleague to prove a new tool before I change the way we fit a frame; I attend our workplace union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the glazing crew a faster order sheet is pleasant, but someone still has to make a window fit a rough opening. Nobody should sell a small office saving as a reason to shorten our paid day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the facade fitting crew and earn the ordinary trade rate; my partner's care work is fairly regular. We have about three months of bills saved for our mortgage and two children, so this picture leaves me comfortable, provided site hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll finish the housing block's window frames and keep using AI now and then to read long specifications. At the next workplace union meeting I'll raise a written rule that a shortened delivery day still brings a minimum paid callout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about fitting work, with the normal attention I give the mortgage. The machine is useful for a page of notes, not for tightening a fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the drawing miss a real opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing gave us a clean rectangle, but the concrete opening leaned. I packed the window frame to the wall we had, then checked the seal before the panel went in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a late glass delivery cut a shift short for two installers. I would bring that date and their lost hours to the union meeting so the paid-callout request is specific.

say: **Window fitting** still needs measured openings and sound seals.
**Office savings** should not shorten the crew's paid day.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and regular care income make mild change manageable.
The **mortgage and children** still make paid site hours important.
do: **Finish** housing block window frames and check each seal.
**Raise** minimum paid callout at next workplace union meeting.
feel: **Calm** about continued fitting work, attentive to paid hours.
S0.quote: I packed the window frame to the wall we had, then checked the seal before the panel went in.
fieldNote: His **high site skill** shows in correcting a leaning opening without treating the drawing as final.
He backs a **union callout rule** with a real lost-hours example, while his current work and moderate reserve support calm.

steps.text: Finish housing block window frames and check seals
Raise minimum paid callout at workplace union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI might take over purchasing and checks before robots can hang a heavy window panel. The fitter should still sign off measurements and the crew should know why the rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own fixing work looks safe in the near term, though faster ordering could tighten shifts around delivery times. My partner's care wage and three-month reserve cover a small interruption, but I would keep an eye on paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare two office-generated glass orders with the measured openings before the truck arrives. If a new AI ordering screen is adopted and a colleague has used it successfully, I'll learn the correction controls on paid time and log any delivery mistakes for the site lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about tighter rosters, not expecting my own income to fall yet. I can accept a proven tool and still insist that a person checks the measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which measurement could a digital order miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure the diagonal as well as the height and width. A rectangular computer sketch can miss a skewed concrete opening and send glass we cannot fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you learn the new ordering screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the colleague to show me one corrected order from an actual site, then practise the edit before the next delivery. If paid time is refused, I will keep sending my measurements to the office.

say: **AI ordering** can help before robots handle heavy window panels.
A fitter should still **sign off measurements** and know about rota changes.
think: My own **fitting wage** looks secure for now.
Tighter **delivery rosters** could create interruptions, cushioned by care income and three months saved.
do: **Compare** two glass orders with measured housing block openings.
**Learn** adopted AI correction controls on paid time after colleague proves them.
feel: **Uneasy** about rosters while current wages still feel safe.
S1.quote: A rectangular computer sketch can miss a skewed concrete opening and send glass we cannot fit.
fieldNote: His new **AI learning** requires an adopted screen, a proven colleague example and paid practice time.
The concern is **potential roster pressure**, while current window fitting and household income remain secure.

steps.text: Compare two glass orders with measured housing block openings
Learn adopted AI correction controls on paid time after colleague demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can order panels and plan facade work, while capable robots around 2031 could put the windows in. We need staffing numbers before people are told to be grateful for a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 48 when robots can do the physical installation. A three-month reserve helps, but losing half my fitting hours would put our mortgage budget under pressure, and only some other local sites need facade crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring the robot timetable question to the union safety group and ask for paid trial observers and written crew numbers. If the firm offers a funded, recognised facade-inspection course with wages during classes, I'll enrol; if my hours are cut, I'll apply only to posted local inspection or fitting jobs with pay covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible hour cut, with time to ask for terms and train. I won't treat a trial invitation as an actual new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the reserve is a bridge, not a replacement for a full wage. We would compare the mortgage payment with one income before deciding whether any course fee is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a paid robot trial test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should fit a panel into an uneven opening with a trained worker able to stop it. Watching a sales film from the yard would not show what happens beside other trades.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans facade work before robots fit windows around 2031.
Workers need **crew numbers** and paid trials before shifts change.
think: At about **48**, losing fitting hours could strain the mortgage.
Our **three-month reserve** and some local sites help, but cannot replace a wage.
do: **Ask** union safety group for robot timetable, paid observers and crew figures.
**Enrol** in funded recognised facade-inspection course if class wages continue.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local fitting or inspection job covering mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours, with training and job options.
S2.quote: A three-month reserve helps, but losing half my fitting hours would put our mortgage budget under pressure, and only some other local sites need facade crews.
fieldNote: His **training action** requires funding, a recognised course and class wages; observing a robot alone is not retraining.
A job move follows **actual hour cuts** and needs a posted local fitting or inspection vacancy with mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Ask union safety group for timetable, paid observers and crew figures
Enrol in funded recognised facade-inspection course if class wages continue
Apply after cuts to posted local fitting or inspection job covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes drawings and orders, then capable robots around 2034 may fit the panels. Five years should let us test a real opening and negotiate a paid transition, if the employer actually means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 51 when site robots do the installation. I'm skilled at awkward openings, but the mortgage still needs the ordinary carpenter wage; five years gives us more time to build a cash cushion from pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will ask the workplace union to seek a written five-year crew plan and funded inspection training with paid release. If a real place and those terms are secured, I'll enrol next intake; we'll also set aside thirty from each full paid week while my care-worker partner and I can cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible later drop in fitting hours, but the longer period gives us room to organise. I want to see a working site trial before changing trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful robot trial look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the robot fit a window into a skewed opening, then test the seal for leaks. A perfect robot test frame would tell me only that the machine can repeat a perfect frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the new weekly deposit come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thirty would come from future wages after our mortgage and children's costs, not from moving the existing reserve. If the site drops a full paid week, we would skip that deposit.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before robots fit windows around 2034.
Workers should demand a **real site trial** and paid transition terms.
think: At about **51**, I may still need the ordinary fitting wage.
Five years could build **new savings** from full paid weeks if household bills allow.
do: **Ask** workplace union for crew plan and funded paid-release inspection course.
**Enrol** next intake if real place, funding and paid release secured.
**Deposit** thirty from each full paid week if household bills allow.
feel: **Anxious** about future hours, with time to organise and save.
S3.quote: A perfect robot test frame would tell me only that the machine can repeat a perfect frame.
fieldNote: He tests site robots against **skewed openings** and needs written funded training with paid release before enrolling.
His **new deposits** use future full-week wages after household bills, not a transfer from the existing three-month reserve.

steps.text: Ask workplace union for crew plan and funded paid-release course
Enrol in inspection course if real place, funding and paid release secured
Deposit thirty from full paid week if household bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may draw the facade and robots around 2039 may put windows in. Ten years is long enough to bargain for proper training and teach younger fitters why a measured opening matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 56 when robots can fit the panels, and I cannot assume the mortgage will be finished. Our three-month reserve and some nearby work give time, yet a later fall in wages is still possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the facade safety ticket current and ask a younger fitter to measure a skewed opening with me on the next block. At the annual union meeting I'll propose a paid handover for apprentices; my partner and I will review the mortgage balance before deciding what further training we can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant wage risk, with time to prepare. I don't need to declare the trade finished while there are windows to fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a younger fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the younger fitter take the diagonal measurement and show how the panel can catch on one corner. A tablet can store a window opening's diagonal, but it does not place the tape on concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the paid handover be arranged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The handover would put paid apprentice hours on the site rota, with a named fitter to sign off each frame. I'd bring an example from our housing block to the union meeting, not just ask for goodwill.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes drawings before robots fit panels around 2039.
A decade allows **paid apprentice handovers** and household review.
think: At about **56**, the mortgage may still require site wages.
Our **moderate reserve** and some nearby firms help, but do not settle future income.
do: **Keep** facade safety ticket current and teach diagonal measurement on site.
**Propose** paid apprentice handover at annual union meeting.
**Review** mortgage balance with partner before choosing further training.
feel: **Uneasy** about later hours, with a practical handover window.
S4.quote: A tablet can store a window opening's diagonal, but it does not place the tape on concrete.
fieldNote: His **site handover** is a real paid rota proposal to the union, not a claim that private coaching is collective action.
He reviews **mortgage figures** without claiming a course place or early retirement at age 56.

steps.text: Keep facade safety ticket current and teach measured openings on site
Propose paid apprentice handover at annual workplace union meeting
Review mortgage balance with partner before choosing further training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because site robots around 2031 could take fitting hours while we still have the mortgage. Written crew numbers, a paid site trial and funded inspection training would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the seal after a robot installs a window on an uneven wall. A window can look straight from the street and still leak into a child's bedroom. The person who signs it off needs time to test it.

headlineQuote: A window can look straight from the street and still leak into a child's bedroom.
portrait: **Liam**, 43, leads facade installation with a vocational trade certificate and strong site skill at ordinary trade pay.
His care-worker partner, two children and **mortgage** share a three-month reserve, with some nearby construction alternatives.
He uses **AI now and then**, waits for proof on real sites and brings paid-hour questions to his workplace union.
Fast site robots make him **anxious** about fitting wages; more time supports funded training, new saving and paid apprentice handovers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring window-fitting robots around 2031 while the mortgage still needs his wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written crew numbers**, a paid site trial and funded inspection training would let him plan before hours fall.
